articles.text: The reported gold discoveries near Bismarck, still create intense excitement. As a speculation we wouldn't give a hundred dollars for all the genuine gold, native to the territory fifty miles around Bismarck. As far as we know or have heard from good sources there is no formation short of the Hills which has ever been found to be gold-bearing.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy scoffs at the excitement over reported gold discoveries near Bismarck.

articles.text: If there is a war with England, the United States and especially the northwest is on the eve of the most prosperous times it has ever seen. We have no great love for England especially since her Egyptian policy was adopted, which, however, is in a line with many of her former wars. Now Russia, Germany and France may singly or together make an attempt to curb the grasping spirit of the English. It is impossible to fully know the status of Europeans affairs but to a man up a tree it looks vastly as though there was going to be a war between England and some other European power or powers. An order received by Swift's and Armour's packing houses in Chicago for 9,500,000 pounds of canned beef to be shipped to Woolwich seems to mean business.
articles.summary: Editorial predicting prosperity for the northwest if England goes to war, citing a huge British order for Chicago canned beef.

articles.text: It is a matter of regret that the laws intended to preserve the game animals of this territory are not more closely observed. It is only a few weeks since three big-horn sheep, all ewes, were brought into town and sold. The man who killed them stated that each ewe carried two lambs. Here was a total of nine lives lost and all for the sum of ten or twelve dollars. Some of our readers are not aware of the stringency of the Dakota game laws. The settler is not allowed to kill game out of season even for his own use. For each sheep, deer, antelope or Buffalo, killed between Jan. 1st. and Sep. 1st. there is a fine of $100 and costs. Elk are cheap as the fine for killing them out of season is only ten dollars and costs. We feel sure that no objections will be made by the people against any man who kills a deer for his own use, but the selling of game out of season, must be stopped. Our large game animals are disappearing very rapidly and it will be but a short time until they are virtually extinct. Only a few years since there were repeatedly seen from fifty to a hundred deer in a day and 300 to 600 antelope but now they are few and far between.
articles.summary: Editorial deploring out-of-season game killing after three pregnant bighorn ewes were sold in town, and warning that large game is nearly gone.

articles.text: The railroad from the Hay creek coal mines into the Hills is now almost an assured fact. This of itself, will not help Medora much, as its general direction will be eastward. In this connection, however we may say that had the Hills merchants stuck to their contract to ship via the N. P., over seventy miles of railroad would already have been built from here south and this year would have seen the other end in the Hills. This was the settled policy of the N. P. and the Hills merchants have only themselves to blame if they are without railroad facilities after this year.
articles.summary: A railroad from the Hay Creek coal mines into the Black Hills is nearly assured, but the paper says it will not help Medora and blames Hills merchants for losing a line south from Medora.

articles.headline: Stock Notes. Strayed or Stolen.
articles.text: From Little Missouri, July 6, 1884, a bay horse, eight years old and weighing about 1,000 pounds. The horse was branded with an anchor on left cheek and a hat brand on left shoulder. On the left hip he had a Texas brand, looking something like 7N, connected with flourish at top of N. A reward of $25 will be paid for information leading to his recovery. The horse is the property of John Pohl, and information can be brought or sent to the Cow Boy office.
articles.summary: John Pohl offers $25 reward for a bay horse strayed or stolen from Little Missouri on July 6, 1884.

articles.headline: The Little Missouri River Stockmen's Association.
articles.text:
In the absence of the chairman Theodore Roosevelt, the convention was called to order by H. S. Boice, vice-chairman.

The following new members were unanimously elected: Griffin Bros. & Ward, J. A. VanEeghan, Pierre Wibaux, E. G. Paddock and John Sawyer.

Willis Eaton moved that J. L. Truscott be elected secretary. Carried.

Howard Eaton moved that a committee of three be selected by the chair to appoint the time, programme and foreman of the spring round-up of this district after first conferring with a similar committee from Glendive and with the round-up committee of the Territorial convention at Miles City. As such committee the chair appointed J. L. Truscott, John Goodall and Wal. Osterhaut.

It was moved by M. A. Griffin that a stock inspector be appointed for Medora and that in case the convention at Miles City refuse to appoint one, that one should be appointed by this association and the expenses be borne pro rata by the members. Carried.

On motion of J. L. Truscott a committee was appointed to see that the above inspector be appointed. The committee consisted of J. M. Simpson, Geo. Towers and Howard Eaton.

The committee appointed to confer with similar committees relative to our round-up were to act in conjunction with the chairman of the meeting and he reported that it was their opinion, having already conferred with the Yellowstone committee, that Wal. T. Osterhaut be appointed foreman and that our round-up begin at the mouth of Box Elder, the point where the upper Little Missouri round-up ends, thence down the river to the motuh of Big Beaver, thence up Big Beaver until the southern Yellowstone round-up is met. The time of the round-up to be decided by the Miles City convention.

It was decided that stockmen on the river should round up the country for about forty miles east of the river and drive the bulk of the cattle back to the river before the general round-up. Adjourned.
articles.summary: Minutes of the Little Missouri River Stockmen's Association meeting, held with chairman Theodore Roosevelt absent: new members, a Medora stock inspector, and the spring round-up plan under foreman Wal. T. Osterhaut.

articles.headline: North of Yellowstone Meeting.
articles.text:
A meeting was held Tuesday afternoon at Glendive by the stockmen holding cattle north of the Yellowstone. It was well attened.

The meeting was called to order by Col. Hodgson who nominated W. W. Newlon for chairman. Carried. W. W. Mabee was then elected sectreary and S. A. Marney and A. T. Packard, vice-presidents.

On motion of Col. Hodgson, Frank Gibson, foreman for Tussler & Co., was elected as foreman of the North Yellowstone round-up.

After considerable discussion as to the most feasible plans it was decided to keep all cattle back from the Yellowstone valley, ten to fifteen miles. Frank Gibson and C. R. A. Scobey, foreman of the Fayette Live Stock Co., were appointed to see that line riders were appointed and did their duty in this respect.

B. Esterbrook moved that the chair select a committee to select another committee to go to Miles and look after the interests of Yellowstone stockmen.

L. P. Williamson moved that bulls be kept off the range between Nov. 1 and July 1, and that a committee be appointed to see that this rule be stricly enforced. During the discussion of this question, which was all favorable, it was brought out that one or two outfits would not comply with the resolution. It was decided to see these firms and if possible, gain unanimous consent to the resolution.
articles.summary: Stockmen north of the Yellowstone met at Glendive Tuesday, electing A. T. Packard a vice-president and Frank Gibson round-up foreman.

articles.text: The cowmen took Medora by storm.
articles.summary: The visiting cowmen filled Medora.

articles.text: The bull round-up north of the track will begin a week from Tuesday.
articles.summary: The bull round-up north of the railroad will begin a week from Tuesday.

articles.text: Politicions could learn a good lesson from the stockmen in running conventions. They all come primed as to what they want, talk it up before the meeting and then rush it through in a hurry.
articles.summary: Quip praising stockmen's efficient conventions.

articles.text: Texas stockmen are seeking relief on all sides from the quarantine laws and will doubtless find it in establishing slaughter-houses and canneries and shipping the beef to Europe
articles.summary: Texas stockmen may answer quarantine laws with slaughter-houses and canneries.

articles.text: Young grass has already started on the slopes of the buttes and the warm rains of April will bring it forth everywhere. There is a well-founded belief that the hay crop this year will be much better than last.
articles.summary: Young grass is up on the butte slopes and a better hay crop is expected.

articles.text: The citizens of Miles City are making great preparations to receive the visiting stockmen tomorrow and it will doubtless be the largest meeting ever held in the northwest outside of Cheyenne. A number of our stockmen will leave tonight for Miles and our interests will be well looked after.
articles.summary: Medora stockmen leave tonight for the big stockmen's convention at Miles City tomorrow.

articles.text: M. Wadsworth returned from the west last evening where he bought a bunch of horses. They are being driven to the ranch by a cowpuncher whom Mr. Wadsworth wants to back against anyone in the Bad Lands at riding or roping. Get out your buckers and reatas, boys.

articles.text: A number of cowmen from the west and south were in attendance at the meeting yesterday. Among them we noticed H. S. Boice, Geo. Towers, Pierre Wibaux, Griffin & Ward, Mr. Rowe, J. N. Simpson and all the stockmen tributary to Medora.
articles.summary: Visiting cowmen at yesterday's stock meeting included H. S. Boice, Geo. Towers, Pierre Wibaux, Griffin & Ward, Mr. Rowe and J. N. Simpson.

articles.text: Whatever can be said against the methods adopted by the "stranglers" who came through here last fall, it cannot but be acknowledged that the result of their work has been very wholesome. Not a definite case of horse stealing from a cowman has been reported since and it seems as though a very thorough cleanup had been made.
articles.summary: The paper credits last fall's vigilante "stranglers" with ending horse stealing from cowmen.

articles.text: Last Friday the Humane Society of Pittsburg entered suit in the United States Court against the Pennsylvania railroad company, alleging that the recent act of Congress, which provides for heavy penalties on all public carriers of live stock for failure to properly care for animals during transportation has been shamelessly disregarded, the defendant company having allowed live stock shipped from Chicago to be on the road sixty-two hours without food, water, or rest. The suit is a test one, and is brought at the suggestion of the agent of the National Humane Society. Should the plaintiffs win the case an attempt will be made to enforce the act in all parts of the United States.—[Kansas City L. S. Indicator.
articles.summary: Reprint: the Humane Society of Pittsburg sued the Pennsylvania railroad over livestock left 62 hours without food or water.

articles.text: Cow horses are in active demand, not only here but through the entire northwest, first class cow horses are bringing from $75 to $80 per head.
articles.summary: First-class cow horses bring $75 to $80 a head.

articles.text: It is reported that the new stock yards for this station are to be built near the old "Y" and will be large enough to hold 5000 cattle. This begins to look as if Medora was to be a shipping point of importance. There are thousands of cattle landed here every spring and this would have been a prominent shipping point last year if there had been any accommodations for that kind of business.
articles.summary: New stock yards holding 5000 cattle are reportedly to be built near the old "Y" at Medora.

articles.text: H. R. Tarbell, Manager of the Little Missouri Horse Co., was in town this week and reports his stock as looking fine. Mr. Tarbell is "pulling the right string" to establish a reputation for fine stock and fair dealing. He wishes it distinctly understood that he is no "jockey" or "horse trader" but solely a breeder and will deal in nothing but the best stock. Stick to it Harry, and you will win not only reputation but in the long run a large and paying business.
articles.summary: H. R. Tarbell of the Little Missouri Horse Co. was in town and reports his stock in fine shape.

articles.text: A Galveston news Wichita Falls special says: Arrangements have been consummated whereby Texas cattle destined for the northern market will be shipped to Harold, the new terminus of the Fort Worth & Denver railroad, thence driven north to Caldwell and Hunnewell, on the south line of Kansas; thence shipped by rail to the destination. Those for Colorado, Wyoming and other northern territories will go from Harold, by way of a new trail, the strip through the north of the Panhandle, and thence north to their respective destinations. This settles the question of an outlet for the cattle drive this year, and saves the Texas stock interests from being seriously crippled though the quarantine laws of Kansas and other states. Whether this scheme will work is hard to tell, but we think the opposition which will come from the ranchmen of the Panhandle, over whose ranges the proposed trail will have to pass, will be so great that it will be found that it is not practicable.—[N. M. Stock Grower.
articles.summary: Reprint on a new trail plan for Texas cattle to reach northern markets.

articles.text: The Northern Pacific has given virtual half-fare rates to all stockmen attending the Miles City meeting. Full fair is to be paid one way and a pass given the other. This applies between, Dickinson, Dakota and Helena, Montana. We are glad to see this evidence of liberality of the Northern Pacific especially as it is in line with a new policy that they have so far been in earnest about adopting. Hitherto, there has been much just cause of complaint and the plain facts have been freely exposed in the columns of the Cow Boy. We are as ready to praise as to condemn and will give the N. P. the credit of now looking to the future for their custom as much as to the present. On all sides can be heard expressions of approval at their un-looked-for liberality and the N. P. seems destined to attain the great praise which it so richly deserves but which it came so near forfeiting.
articles.summary: The Northern Pacific gives stockmen half-fare to the Miles City meeting, and the Cow Boy praises the railroad's new liberality.

articles.text: There is a point concerning the detection of stock thieves which we think has escaped the notice of editors. It is in relation to the capture of the thieves. Of course it is necessary to advertise the loss immediately and as widely as possible, as this alone very often leads to detection. Where the thief has gotten away with his booty, however, nothing should be said as to the means being employed to bring the culprit to justice as this is one of the most certain means toward making escape easier. An instance was brought to our mind by the Atchison Champion. It seems that a man named Griffith, an ex-sheriff, had sold a lot of cattle and then skipped to parts unknown. Thus far the article is all right and by the right kind of advertising the thief would almost surely have been cought. The article further says, however, that the losers by this steal had selected one of their number to catch Griffith and that he proposed going to his old home and see if he did not turn up there. If is manifest that a man in Griffith's position will keep well posted and the agent could as well look for Griffith to show up at his old home as he could for him to appear in the moon. It is a very easy thing for a paper to say too much as has doubtless been done in this case.
articles.summary: Editorial advising papers not to publish how stock thieves are being pursued, citing an Atchison Champion story.

articles.headline: Smiles. He Was Sorry.
articles.text:
Smiles.

He Was Sorry.

The other morning a tramp walked up to one of our prominent citizens on the street and, shivering with cold, begged him for a quarter with which to buy something to eat. The prominent citizen stopped and looked at his trampship pityingly, then replied:

"My good man, how long is it since you had a meal?"

"Two days," said the tramp, as his kneees shook and his teeth chattered.

"I am very sorry, my friend, but I have not had a dinner for two weeks." The tramp opened his eyes and looked wild, and his teeth ceased chattering and his knees no longer quaked as he drew breath with difficulty and sadly said:

"Here is a quarter, poor fellow. Take it and go and get some grub."

"But I am not a beggar!" cried the prominent citizen.

"I know, I know," the tramp replied, "but you are the champion liar of the country. You were picking your teeth when I met you."—[Bloomington Through Mail.
articles.summary: Reprinted humor item about a tramp and a prominent citizen.

articles.text: Our respected and versatile hardware merchant has just received an extensive consignment of papers through the mail. It is presumed that they were delayed by the recent eclipse of the sun, as some of them are of rather ancient date.

articles.text: E. G. Paddock's new livery and sale stable is nearly completed and will be a great convenience as well as an ornament to the town. He will no doubt reap a liberal harvest from the tourists trade this summer as well as from the local trade.

articles.text: The managers of the rink have decided to make the price for admision and skates as follows: Gentlemen, admission twenty-five cents, skates 10 cents; ladies, admission free, skates twenty-five cents. articles.summary: The skating rink announces admission and skate prices.

articles.headline: high
articles.text: Rev. W. B. Schaffner, of Dic[kin?]son, preached an eloquent serm[on?] in [th?]e rink last Sunday evening. There was a good audience, which listened attentively to the minister's words. Mr. Schaffner will preach here again a week from Sunday evening at half-past seven in the rink. There is no doubt that a large audience will turn out.
articles.summary: Rev. W. B. Schaffner of Dickinson preached in the rink Sunday and will return a week from Sunday.

articles.text: All those intending to take part in the skating masquerade and carnival April 15, should be practicing as much as possible beforehand so that they won't fall down and break their masks that evening. If you cannot afford a special costume for the evening, don't let that keep you from taking part in the festivities. Our worthy "six eyed" gentleman will have masks for sale at the confectionery and news depot. The masks will cost about twenty-five cents each. An old cotton umbrella and a plug hat makes a very good masquerade costume. That is, in connection with other necessary wearing apparel. However, to avoid monotony, we would suggest that this costume be not universally adopted.
articles.summary: Skaters are urged to prepare for the April 15 skating masquerade and carnival; masks sold at the confectionery.

articles.text:
The shoot last Saturday was a disappointment as far as scores were concerned. It was the worst shooting we have yet had, the only redeeming feature being Peter Book's hundred yard score.

The day was almost perfect for shooting, the weather fine and hardly a breath of air stirring. Almost all the contestants claimed to be in good trim for shooting and then would step up and miss the target. There is something about shooting which cannot be explained and still it will make a whole team shoot poorly. We cannot imagine what it is, but below is seen the result. It might be added that the target is the regulation army one of an eight-inch bulls eye at the three ranges.

Since the above was put in type, it was found to be impossible to give the score in full this issue. The next shoot will decide the winner of the gun, when the complete scores will be published.
articles.summary: Saturday's rifle shoot produced poor scores except Peter Book's at 100 yards; the next shoot will decide the gun.

articles.text: Crossings of the Little Missouri can now be made wherever there is a ford.
articles.summary: The Little Missouri can now be forded at any ford.

articles.text: Two or three drain ditches are badly needed. They will doubtless be put in this summer.
articles.summary: Drain ditches are needed in town.

articles.text: A petition in opposition to the removal of the post-office from its present location was numerously signed yesterday.
articles.summary: A petition against moving the post-office was widely signed.

articles.text: Roberts & Townsend's outfit loaded and pulled for the Hills yesterday afternoon, with about 50,000 pounds of freight.
articles.summary: Roberts & Townsend's freight outfit left for the Black Hills with 50,000 pounds.

articles.text: The brush is all being cleared away east and north of the slaughter-house and the appearance of the town is much improved thereby.
articles.summary: Brush is being cleared around the slaughter-house.

articles.text: Thomas Gibson, who was killed by a bear down the river, worked for Peter Book last summer and came here from the Hills. Perhaps the Hills papers could find some information about him.
articles.summary: Thomas Gibson, a former employee of Peter Book, was killed by a bear down the river.

articles.text: Frank Walker, who shot himself in the leg some time ago, died this morning and will be buried at four o'clock this afternoon. Blood poisoning was the immediate cause of his death. Walker was not a good patient, being very fretful but was probably more or less out of his head all the time. Once, being alone he got out of bed and hurt himself badly.
articles.summary: Frank Walker died of blood poisoning from a self-inflicted leg wound and is buried this afternoon.

articles.headline: Notice.
articles.text:
Notice.

Notice is hereby given that any contracts or bills made by any of the employes of the Medora Stage and Forwarding Co., will not be paid or recognized unless approved by W. F. Van Driesche, Treasurer.

Marquis de Mores, Pres't.
articles.summary: The Medora Stage and Forwarding Co. will honor no employee bills unless approved by treasurer W. F. Van Driesche.
